body:
# Independent audit of sector feasibility, with singular rigidity

This note audits the ordinary planar statements in
`candidate be9098c627b40217`,
`candidate 697de064a9368ba1`, and
`candidate 2e26c63010f03ffc`.
It then proves an actual-body rigidity consequence and a precisely scoped
finite-data optimizer consequence. None of these statements preserves
compatibility between distinct mixed-integer fibers.

## 1. Data and audit conclusion

Let m>=3. Let P_i be nonzero points on distinct cyclically ordered rays
covering the plane, with each consecutive angular gap below pi. Indices
are cyclic. Prescribe sector areas A_i, and put

    D_i=det(P_i,P_(i+1))>0,
    E_i=det(P_(i-1),P_(i+1)),
    kappa_i=D_(i-1)+D_i-E_i,
    t_i=2A_i/D_i>=1,                 a_i=t_i-1,
    h_i=a_i/(D_i t_i),               b_i=kappa_i/(D_(i-1)D_i).

Define the symmetric matrix L by

    x^T L x=sum_i b_i x_i^2-sum_i h_i(x_i+x_(i+1))^2.       (1)

The three sources pass an independent line-by-line audit. Precisely, the
data are realized by a convex body containing zero in its interior if
and only if L is positive semidefinite. The source's finite construction
is valid even with zero excesses, disconnected positive-edge graphs, or
a singular matrix. The following details are material to this conclusion.

* The first source preserves a separately chosen actual supporting line
  at every P_i, not merely the radial endpoints and sector areas. Its
  bounded and unbounded support-wedge constructions both produce the
  exact sector area. The global gauge proof supplies convexity across
  the prescribed rays.
* The second source computes the exact joining condition

      D_i a_(i-1)/u_(i-1)+D_(i-1)a_i/v_i<=kappa_i,        (2)

  where u_i,v_i>0 and u_i+v_i=t_i. It neither infers global convexity
  from separate convex sectors nor assumes that the original body is
  polygonal. The extra sector point is V_i=u_i P_i+v_i P_(i+1).
* With r_i=a_i/(D_i u_i), s_i=a_i/(D_i v_i), positive-excess edges obey

      r_i s_i/(r_i+s_i)=h_i,
      r_(i-1)+s_i<=b_i.                                (3)

  Zero excess has h_i=r_i=s_i=0 and can use u_i=v_i=1/2.
* The relaxed edge constraints r,s>=h and (r-h)(s-h)>=h^2 form a closed
  convex set. Scaling both charges down restores the exact harmonic
  equality and lowers both node loads. At h=0 both charges may be set
  to zero. Thus no relaxation gap appears.
* The upward set of feasible finite node budgets is closed: convergent
  budgets uniformly bound every nonnegative charge by one of those
  budgets. Finite-dimensional subsequential convergence applies to the
  actual charge vectors. Nearest-point separation supplies a
  nonnegative separating vector without a strict-feasibility premise.
* The exact dual edge infimum is

      h_i(sqrt(theta_i)+sqrt(theta_(i+1)))^2.

  If one theta vanishes and h_i>0, this need not be attained. The source
  correctly uses only the infimum and does not claim finite attainment
  for that dual edge. Closedness of the primal budget set independently
  supplies a finite feasible charge vector when all dual tests pass.
* The matrix has nonpositive off-diagonal entries. Consequently
  x^T L x>=|x|^T L |x|. Copositivity is therefore precisely positive
  semidefiniteness here, with no omitted sign cases.

There is also a direct finite reconstruction. On each connected
positive-h block, a least Rayleigh eigenvector can be chosen nonnegative
by taking absolute values. A zero entry would force all its positive-edge
neighbors to vanish by the eigen-equation, hence would force the entire
connected vector to vanish. Thus the vector is strictly positive. A
singleton uses the entry one. Positive semidefiniteness gives a combined
vector w>0 with Lw>=0. Set

    r_i=h_i(1+w_i/w_(i+1)),
    s_i=h_i(1+w_(i+1)/w_i),
    u_i=t_i w_(i+1)/(w_i+w_(i+1)),
    v_i=t_i w_i/(w_i+w_(i+1))                            (4)

on positive edges. Equations (2) and (3) follow directly. On zero edges
use zero charges and u_i=v_i=1/2. All coordinates are finite and positive.

Conversely, define node slacks delta_i=b_i-r_(i-1)-s_i>=0.
The charge orientation in the following identity is exact:

    x^T L x=sum_i delta_i x_i^2
       +sum_(h_i>0) (s_i x_i-r_i x_(i+1))^2/(r_i+s_i).    (5)

Expanding a single edge gives coefficients s_i-h_i at x_i^2,
r_i-h_i at x_(i+1)^2, and -2h_i at x_i x_(i+1), which combine with
the node slacks to give (1). This also proves necessity directly.

## 2. Singular strict-excess data determine the actual body

**Theorem 1.** Assume all A_i>D_i/2, so all h_i>0. If L is positive
semidefinite and singular, exactly one convex body realizes the stated
radial endpoints and sector areas. It is an m-vertex polygon. Every P_i
lies in the relative interior of one of its edges, and its vertices are
the points V_i given by (4), where w is any positive null vector of L.

**Proof.** The positive-edge graph is now the connected cycle. A least
Rayleigh eigenvector is strictly positive by the argument above. Since
L is positive semidefinite and singular, its least eigenvalue is zero;
write this vector as w>0 with Lw=0.

Take any feasible exact charges (3), obtained for example from any
one-extra-vertex realization. Evaluating (5) at w shows that a sum of
nonnegative terms is zero. Hence

    delta_i=0,                 s_i w_i=r_i w_(i+1)        (6)

for every i. The harmonic equality in (3) and these ratios uniquely give
the first two formulas in (4), and therefore uniquely give u_i,v_i and
V_i. In particular every one-extra-vertex realization is the same
polygon P.

The zero node slack means equality in (2). Therefore the consecutive
boundary pieces V_(i-1)--P_i--V_i are collinear. The global convex
polygon construction makes P_i lie between V_(i-1) and V_i. Each V_i
belongs to the open angular sector between P_i and P_(i+1), so neither
incident piece can have zero length. Thus P_i is in the relative
interior of that straight edge. At V_i the turning determinant is

    det(V_i-P_i,P_(i+1)-V_i)=D_i(t_i-1)>0.

Consequently precisely the V_i are the vertices, and P has m vertices.

It remains to prove rigidity of every actual realizing body, rather
than only uniqueness within the polygonal representations. Let K be
any realizing convex body. Choose one supporting line of K at each
P_i. The support-preserving replacement theorem supplies a
one-extra-vertex polygon with the same data and with all of those
chosen lines still supporting it. The preceding uniqueness makes that
replacement equal to P. Since P_i is in the relative interior of an
edge of P, its supporting line is unique. Therefore each chosen line
is exactly the corresponding edge line of P. The body K lies in each
of its supporting halfplanes, and their intersection is P. Thus K is
contained in P.

Both bodies have total area sum_i A_i, because the finitely many sector
boundaries have zero planar area. Inclusion of convex bodies with equal
area implies equality. Indeed, if K were a proper closed subset of P,
a point of P outside K could be strictly separated from K, leaving a
positive-area portion of the full-dimensional convex body P outside K.
This contradicts equal area. Hence K=P.

The formulas do not depend on scaling w. In fact the nullspace is
one-dimensional: (5), with the charges from (4), forces every null
vector x to satisfy x_i/w_i=x_(i+1)/w_(i+1) on every edge. Connectivity
makes all these ratios equal. This completes the proof. QED.

The strict-excess hypothesis is essential to the stated form: zero
edges may disconnect the graph and allow sectors or joins not governed
by this single positive null vector. No classification of those more
general singular cases is asserted here.

## 3. A finite-data inverse-chord optimizer lies on the matrix boundary

Fix N>=2 distinct lines through zero, giving m=2N cyclic rays with
consecutive gaps below pi. On ray i write P_i=R_i e_i, where the
directions e_i are fixed and R_i>0 varies. For line j, let its chord
length in a fixed normalization be

    ell_j=c_j(R_j+R_(j+N)),             c_j>0.

The constants may, for example, convert the fixed radial parameter to
Euclidean length or to a fixed coarea length. Define the normalized
inverse weight of a target line j by

    p_j=(1/ell_j)/(sum_(l=1)^N 1/ell_l).                  (7)

Let any admissibility conditions, in addition to radial/sector
realizability, depend only on the sector-area vector (A_i). These may
include equalities or closed inequalities; no strictness of those
area-only conditions is required.

**Theorem 2.** A local minimum of p_j in the finite data (R_i,A_i) cannot
have L positive definite. This exclusion does not require strict sector
excesses. If all sector excesses at the minimum are strictly positive,
its realizing body is the unique 2N-vertex polygon in Theorem 1. The same
conclusions hold at an attained global minimum among all realizing
convex bodies under the stated area-only conditions.

**Proof.** Suppose L is positive definite. Choose a ray on a line l
different from the target line j, and decrease its positive radius by
a sufficiently small positive amount. Leave all A_i and all other
radii fixed. Only the two consecutive determinants incident to that
ray change, and both decrease while staying positive. Thus every
core-area inequality A_i>=D_i/2 remains true, including any equality.
The entries of L vary continuously, and positive definiteness is open,
so the new L remains positive definite. The exact criterion therefore
realizes the perturbed data by an actual convex body. Every area-only
constraint is unchanged exactly.

Only ell_l decreases. Its reciprocal strictly increases, while the
positive numerator 1/ell_j and all other terms in the denominator of
(7) remain fixed. Hence p_j strictly decreases. The perturbed data converge to the original
data, contradicting a finite-data local minimum. A global body minimum
is also contradicted, since the realizing perturbed body is admissible
and has a smaller objective. At a feasible minimum L is positive
semidefinite; once positive definiteness is excluded it is singular.
If every excess is positive, Theorem 1 applies. QED.

For three lines this gives a genuine six-vertex polygon at every
strict-excess optimizer in the stated sense. It does not give a
triangle. The proof does not assert the conclusion for a merely
Hausdorff-local optimizer among arbitrary convex bodies: the exact
feasibility criterion alone does not ensure that its polygonal
reconstructions approach an arbitrary original body in Hausdorff
distance. Nor does it permit constraints on other fiber shapes,
Minkowski compatibility, additional support values, or prescribed
chord weights to be ignored.
